title: Solve the 0/1 Knapsack problem bottom-up with a table instead of recursion, then reduce the table to a single row. Explain the recurrence, the reverse-capacity iteration, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: 0/1 Knapsack Tabulation (Bottom-Up Table with Space Optimisation)

s1_definition.profdef: The tabulated 0/1 Knapsack fills a table where each cell holds the best value using the first i items within a capacity c. Each cell chooses the better of excluding item i, copying the value from the row above, or including item i, adding its value to the cell for the reduced capacity in the row above. The table reduces to one row iterated in reverse capacity order so each item is used at most once.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India allocates a fixed capital budget across one-time loan deals, each either fully funded or skipped. We build a table of best profit for every budget level as we consider each deal, then collapse it to a single running row.
s1_definition.oneliner: Fill best-value cells bottom-up, and with one row iterate capacity downward so each item is used once.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The tabulated 0/1 Knapsack fills a table where each cell holds the best value using the first i items within a capacity c. Each cell chooses the better of excluding item i, copying the value from the row above, or including item i, adding its value to the cell for the reduced capacity in the row above. The table reduces to one row iterated in reverse capacity order so each item is used at most once.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India allocates a fixed capital budget across one-time loan deals, each either fully funded or skipped. We build a table of best profit for every budget level as we consider each deal, then collapse it to a single running row.

**One line to remember:** Fill best-value cells bottom-up, and with one row iterate capacity downward so each item is used once.

sections.s2_technical:
The two-dimensional recurrence says the best value using the first i items at capacity c is the maximum of two options. Excluding item i copies the value from the cell directly above, meaning the best using the first i minus one items at the same capacity. Including item i, allowed only if its weight is at most c, adds its value to the cell above at capacity c minus its weight. We fill the table row by row, and the bottom-right cell is the answer.

The one-row optimisation is `for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) for (int c = cap; c >= weight[i]; c--) dp[c] = Math.max(dp[c], value[i] + dp[c - weight[i]]);`. The capacity loop must run downward so that `dp[c - weight[i]]` still refers to the previous item's value, which enforces using each item at most once; iterating upward would allow reusing the same item and silently solve the unbounded knapsack instead. A concrete check: with weights 1, 3, 4, 5 and values 1, 4, 5, 7 and capacity 7, the final `dp[7]` is nine. Senior nuance: the time is items times capacity and the space drops from items times capacity down to just capacity with the single-row trick.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India must allocate a fixed capital budget across a set of one-time loan deals, where each deal is either fully funded or skipped and promises a fixed profit for a fixed capital cost. The bank wants the maximum total profit within the budget, computed without deep recursion so it is safe for large deal lists. This is exactly how the tabulated 0/1 Knapsack works: build the best-profit table bottom-up and collapse it to one row.

The code defines a `CapitalAllocationService` with `bestProfit(capital, profit, budget)` using the single-row reverse iteration. A `Demo` provides deals and logs the best profit.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is four deals with capital one, three, four, five and profit one, four, five, seven, and a budget of seven. Step 1: we create a single row of eight profit cells all initialised to zero. Step 2: processing the first deal of capital one, we walk capacity from seven down to one, setting each cell to one wherever the budget allows. Step 3: processing the deal of capital three profit four, the downward walk updates cells using the previous row's values, so no deal is double-counted. Step 4: processing the deal of capital four profit five, cell seven becomes the best of its current value and five plus the cell at capacity three, which already holds four, giving nine. Step 5: processing the deal of capital five profit seven does not beat nine at capacity seven. Step 6: the final cell at budget seven holds nine, the maximum allocated profit.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The tabulated 0/1 Knapsack turns the recursive include-or-exclude logic into a bottom-up table, and the recurrence is exactly the same choice expressed over a grid. The best value using the first i items at capacity c is the larger of excluding item i, which copies the value from the row above at the same capacity, or including item i when it fits, which adds its value to the row above at the capacity reduced by its weight. I fill the grid row by row and read the answer from the bottom-right cell.

The part interviewers really want to hear is the space optimisation and why the loop direction matters. Because each row depends only on the row immediately above, I can collapse the whole grid into a single row. The catch is that when I update a cell I must read an older value that belongs to the previous item, so I iterate the capacity from high down to low. If I iterated upward I would read a value that was already updated for the current item, which would let me use the same item multiple times and silently turn it into the unbounded knapsack.

At the National Bank of India I used this to allocate a fixed capital budget across one-time loan deals, each either fully funded or skipped, computing the maximum total profit without any recursion so it stayed safe for large deal lists. I kept a single profit row sized to the budget and walked the capacity downward for each deal. Explaining the grid recurrence, the collapse to one row, and the crucial downward capacity loop that keeps it a 0/1 problem is what shows an interviewer I truly understand bottom-up knapsack.
